text: Qiskit never needed an interop lesson, because Qiskit is Python — there's no boundary to cross. Q# is a separate compiled language, which means calling it from Python is a real, deliberate integration step, not an implicit given. This lesson is that step.

Four things to understand: mixing Q# and Python is a genuinely different problem than anything Qiskit-only work requires, because your quantum logic lives in a separate, statically-typed, compiled language with its own type system. The qsharp Python package is the bridge — the percent-percent-qsharp cell magic in a notebook, followed by qsharp.eval from an ordinary Python cell. And results come back as native Python objects, with no manual serialization step on your part.

In a Jupyter notebook, the percent-percent-qsharp cell magic lets you write and compile Q# source directly. The operation compiles the moment that cell runs, and qsharp.eval calls it by name and hands the return value straight back into Python — you can print it, check its type, branch on it, exactly like any other Python value.

A single call only gives you one measurement. To see the real distribution, call it repeatedly from a Python loop and tally the outcomes with a Counter — exactly the orchestration Python is good at and Q# isn't trying to replace. Since PrepareAndMeasure applies H to |0> before measuring, the theoretically expected distribution is exactly fifty-fifty, verified directly by squaring the amplitude one over root two. A real run over a thousand shots lands near, but not exactly at, five hundred and five hundred — sampling variation around that true split.

Next lesson goes beyond calling one operation at a time — into the real workflow: target profiles, native repeated sampling, pulling resource estimates into the same Python session, and handing a validated program off to Azure Quantum.
